title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
The wind-resource calculation converts hourly wind speed and direction into a compact probability model. The wake model uses this distribution to calculate annual energy production, while the hydrogen calculations use the same distribution to weight part-load operating states.
The model retains direction because farm power depends on the alignment between the wind and turbine rows. A single all-direction Weibull distribution would remove that dependency.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Direction Sectors
The legacy fitting script divides wind direction \(\theta\) into twelve 30-degree sectors. The stored label is the lower edge of each sector:
\[
s(\theta)
=30^\circ\left\lfloor
\frac{\theta\bmod 360^\circ}{30^\circ}
\right\rfloor.
\]
Sector \(s=0^\circ\) therefore contains observations from \(0^\circ\) up to, but not including, \(30^\circ\). If \(n_s\) is the number of valid observations in sector \(s\) and \(N_\mathrm{obs}\) is the total number of observations, the direction probability is:
\[
p_s=\frac{n_s}{N_\mathrm{obs}},
\qquad
\sum_s p_s=1.
\]
The sector labels are passed directly to the wake model as wind directions. Because the label is a bin edge rather than its centre, the represented direction may be displaced by 15 degrees from the observations in that bin. This is retained here to document the legacy calculation and identified below as a required correction.

title: Wind Resource and Weibull Distribution
text:
Conditional Weibull Distribution
Wind speed \(v\) within each direction sector is represented by a two-parameter Weibull distribution with shape \(k_s\) and scale \(c_s\). The location parameter is fixed at zero. The cumulative distribution and probability density are:
\[
F_s(v)
=1-\exp\left[-\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s}\right],
\]
\[
f_s(v)
=\frac{k_s}{c_s}
\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s-1}
\exp\left[-\left(\frac{v}{c_s}\right)^{k_s}\right],
\]
where \(v\) and \(c_s\) are in m/s and \(k_s\) is dimensionless. The fitting script estimates \(k_s\) and \(c_s\) by maximum likelihood using scipy.stats.weibull_min.fit with the location fixed at zero.
For a speed bin bounded by \(v_i\) and \(v_{i+1}\), the joint probability of direction sector \(s\) and that speed bin is:
\[
w_{s,i}
=p_s\left[F_s(v_{i+1})-F_s(v_i)\right].
\]
This joint probability is the weight applied to the corresponding wake-aware farm-power or conversion state.

title: Turbine System
text:
The turbine-system model calculates the mass and supply cost of one offshore wind turbine and its monopile foundation. It retains component masses because they connect turbine design to foundation sizing, transport, lifting, and installation-vessel requirements.
The model boundary includes the rotor, nacelle, turbine electrical equipment, tower, monopile, and a transition-piece supply allowance. It excludes offshore transport and installation, scour protection, array infrastructure, export infrastructure, and hydrogen-production equipment. Where architecture-specific equipment is supported by the turbine foundation, its mass is passed into the foundation calculation without moving its cost into the turbine-system boundary.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
This research compares two energy carriers for offshore wind — electricity and hydrogen — by designing a complete energy system around each and placing the results side by side. The carrier is the one choice fixed in advance, deliberately, because it is the variable under study. Everything downstream of that choice is left free: generation, collection, conversion, transport, storage, and delivery are designed as one coupled problem, and each carrier gets the architecture that suits it best rather than the architecture built for the other.
Two things distinguish this from most existing techno-economic work on offshore wind and its carrier options. First, scope of the design variables. Many studies comparing transport methods or conversion routes hold turbine spacing, power density, and layout fixed as inputs. Here they are outputs of the same design problem as everything else, because they are physically coupled to it: export capacity depends on how power is aggregated, which depends on where conversion happens, which depends on spacing, which sets the wake losses that shape the production profile the rest of the chain has to handle. Fixing any one of these while designing the rest quietly fixes an assumption the comparison should instead be free to test. Second, scope of the chain itself. The comparison runs through the full chain to delivery, not to the offshore/onshore interface. Where the demand being served is electrical, reconversion equipment and losses belong on the ledger exactly as much as export cables do. Nothing is compared at a midpoint that happens to flatter one option over the other. What that demand consists of — its composition, location, and timing — is not fixed by the research but specified per scenario, so that the comparison can be drawn for different end-uses on the same transparent terms.
The comparison is deliberately between pure systems. Hybrid configurations, in which both carriers leave the farm side by side, are excluded by design — not because they are implausible, but because the question here is comparative rather than global. The aim is not to find the single best North Sea system; it is to isolate what each carrier’s cost structure does to the optimal design when the system is organized entirely around it. A hybrid would blur exactly the contrast the research is built to expose, and the two pure systems bound the space in which any hybrid would sit.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
section: Why efficiency is not the objective
text:
Why efficiency is not the objective
This is not a new problem for engineers. A plant built from locally efficient unit operations is not guaranteed to be the cheapest plant to build and run, which is precisely why process design happens at the flowsheet level, not unit by unit. Offshore energy systems have the same structure, and the carrier question is where it shows up most clearly.
Converting electricity to hydrogen and back loses energy that direct electrification does not. That is the correct, uncontested thermodynamic argument, and nothing here disputes it. What is in question is whether it is the right variable to optimize, as opposed to one cost among several to be weighed. A conversion loss is a cost like any other. It can be outweighed by savings elsewhere in the chain, the same way a less efficient piece of equipment can still be the cheaper one to own if it needs less supporting infrastructure around it.
Widen the accounting to the full chain and both carriers show a side that a production-level comparison can’t capture. Electricity’s costs surface downstream, and they come from more than one place. Transmission infrastructure is priced by peak capacity (€/MW) while revenue is earned per delivered MWh. That mismatch alone pushes designs toward protecting utilization: wider spacing, lower installed density, export links sized below peak generation, curtailment by design. A second, independent driver pushes the same way. Wind production and demand rarely line up in time, and because large-scale electrical storage is expensive, the surplus generated in high-production periods has nowhere economical to go and gets curtailed rather than stored. How large that mismatch is depends on the demand profile the system serves; curtailment is evaluated here against exogenous demand profiles, and results are read as conditional on them, with sensitivity to their shape part of the analysis. Neither driver requires the other: capacity could be perfectly sized and curtailment would still happen on the mismatch alone, just as it would happen on the capacity mismatch even with perfectly aligned demand. Both are invisible at the farm gate, where a MWh produced and a MWh delivered are treated as the same thing. High efficiency at the wire can coexist with high infrastructure cost per delivered MWh and low spatial yield.
Hydrogen’s costs and benefits both surface downstream, not just its benefits. Conversion losses are immediate and local, exactly where the thermodynamic argument places them, and if the end-use is electrical, a second conversion loss and its equipment show up again at the far end of the chain. None of that is waived. What also shows up downstream, and what a farm-gate comparison structurally can’t see, is cheaper bulk pipeline transport, cheaper large-scale storage, and export capacity that can be added more gradually than electrical capacity typically allows. A comparison drawn at the farm gate registers hydrogen’s losses and registers none of the rest, in either direction, for either carrier.
Efficiency, in other words, is an instrumental variable, not a terminal one. What is terminal is the cost of energy delivered to the end-user and the sea area required to produce it (MWh/km²), and neither outranks the other by default. Cost is the more familiar objective, so it is worth stating plainly why space carries equal weight here rather than trailing behind it as a footnote. The North Sea is not an empty canvas: shipping lanes, fishing grounds, cables, pipelines, defence areas, and nature protection all compete for the same seabed, and the area allocated to wind development is being fixed now, in blocks, for decades. A design that trades a little energy density for a large reduction in €/MWh is a good answer to a cost-minimization problem and can be a poor one where space is the binding constraint. Which of the two binds first is itself an outcome of architecture and carrier choice, not a fixed fact about the wind resource. Rather than collapsing the two into a single number, results are presented as cost–density trade-offs per carrier, so that the balance between them stays visible instead of being decided inside the model.
Whether the most efficient design is also the cheapest and most space-effective one is not something to assume in either direction. It’s the empirical question this research is built to answer.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Research question and expected mechanism

How does the choice of energy carrier alter subsystem-level marginal cost structures, and how does this reshape the economically optimal offshore wind farm design and the achievable energy density (MWh/km²)?

The expected mechanism is this: the optimal design balances the marginal cost of expanding capacity-rated infrastructure (∂C/∂MW) against the marginal value of delivered energy (€/MWh), and the carrier determines where that balance sits. Where capacity expansion is expensive and discrete, the optimum is expected to shift toward utilization preservation at the expense of installed density; where capacity scales gradually, higher density can remain optimal. Energy density would then be an emergent outcome of system design, not a fixed property of the wind resource, and it may differ by carrier. Whether it does, and by how much, is what the comparison is built to show.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
section: The comparison: electricity versus hydrogen as the primary carrier
text:
The comparison: electricity versus hydrogen as the primary carrier
The central comparison places two fully worked-out systems side by side, each designed end-to-end around its own carrier:
Electricity as primary carrier. Power is aggregated electrically, transmitted onshore via standardized high-capacity HVDC blocks, and converted downstream where needed. This is the current North Sea planning paradigm, built on centralized aggregation and bespoke offshore platforms.
Hydrogen as primary carrier. Electrolysis takes place at or near each turbine, and hydrogen, not electricity, is the medium in which energy is collected, transported, and stored. Restructuring around the carrier replaces heavy central aggregation with modular, repeatable conversion units (economies of series rather than scale), collection networks that follow pipeline rather than cable logic, and peak formation, reliability, and storage dynamics distributed across many small units instead of concentrated in one platform.
Hydrogen is worth testing not because it is more efficient — it is not — but because of what sits downstream of the conversion: bulk transport by pipeline, storage at large scale, and export capacity added gradually, all far cheaper than their electrical equivalents. The conversion loss is the price paid for that cheaper chain, which is why the version worth comparing is a farm rebuilt around hydrogen’s downstream economics, not electrolysers added to an electric one.
Each system is designed on its own terms. Neither carrier is evaluated inside an architecture built for the other, which is the comparison this research is designed to avoid.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Method
The comparison is implemented as an integrated techno-economic model of the full chain, from wind resource to delivery. Rather than searching for a single mathematical optimum, the model calculates a wide range of designs for each carrier — varying spacing, conversion siting, export sizing, storage, and the other design variables together — across scenarios for wind climate, distance to shore, institutional block sizes, demand profiles, and financing. The aim is to map where the good designs lie for each carrier and how that map shifts as conditions change, not to pin down a precise best point. Robustness is judged by whether those qualitative patterns persist across the scenario range, not by point-estimate precision.
Market dynamics and price formation are outside the scope: the framing throughout is that a given demand is met at the lowest total system cost. This excludes revenue-side effects — such as the value of selling into high-price hours — for both carriers symmetrically, and keeps the comparison a question of infrastructure cost rather than market behaviour.
The dissertation is deliberately model-first rather than papers-first: the subsystems are so tightly coupled (spacing → wakes → production profile → conversion sizing → export sizing → cost → back to spacing) that isolated component studies would require freezing exactly the variables the research treats as free. The integrated model is the engine from which the papers derive.

title: Electricity and Hydrogen: Comparing Energy Carriers for Offshore Wind, over the entire value chain
text:
Why this matters now
Investment and planning decisions for offshore energy infrastructure are being made now, on multi-decade horizons, under the working assumption that architecture is close to fixed and only production-level parameters remain to be optimized. If that assumption doesn’t hold — if the coupling between spacing, conversion siting, export sizing, and carrier choice materially changes the optimal design — the cost of finding out late is high: offshore infrastructure is expensive to redo and effectively impossible to change once built. Putting the two carriers on equal footing, each with the system that suits it best, and making the comparison explicit and testable now rather than leaving it implicit, is what this research is for.

title: System Boundary and LCOE
text:
The model boundary runs from wind turbine generation to the onshore delivery point. It includes turbines, foundations, infield collection, offshore platforms or substations, conversion equipment, export infrastructure, and onshore conversion or delivery interface.
This boundary is used because offshore electricity and offshore hydrogen differ mainly in the infrastructure required between the turbine and the shore. Excluding export infrastructure would make the comparison structurally biased toward electricity, because the electrical pathway would be evaluated before its largest carrier-specific cost items enter the calculation.

title: System Boundary and LCOE
text:
LCOE Definition
The levelised cost of energy is calculated as annualised lifetime cost divided by annual delivered energy:
LCOE = annualised_cost / annual_energy_delivered
For electricity configurations, delivered energy is electrical energy at the onshore grid connection point. For hydrogen configurations, hydrogen yield is converted to energy using the higher heating value.

title: System Boundary and LCOE
text:
Conceptual Cost Structure
The model uses the following conceptual decomposition to explain why infrastructure affects optimal design:
LCOE = C1 / Yield + C2 / Capacity Factor + C3
where:

C1 represents fixed project costs that do not scale strongly with installed capacity or yield.
C2 represents capacity-linked infrastructure costs, such as turbines, foundations, converters, platforms, cables, electrolysers, compressors, and pipelines.
C3 represents energy-linked costs or losses, including conversion penalties and variable operating costs.

This is a conceptual expression, not the full implementation. Its role is to show why a high cost per MW of infrastructure penalises low-capacity-factor designs: infrastructure is sized for peak power, while revenue and LCOE recovery depend on delivered annual energy.

title: Optimisation Variables
text:
Layout Variables
Turbine spacing and wind farm power density determine the trade-off between areal yield and capacity factor. Tighter spacing increases installed capacity per area but increases wake losses. Wider spacing improves capacity factor but lowers MWh/km2.

Hydrogen Variables
For hydrogen configurations, the main optimisation variables are:

The stack overplant factor affects both conversion efficiency and CAPEX. Oversizing the stack lowers current density and can improve efficiency, but increases stack CAPEX.
Pipeline pressure and diameter affect both transport capacity and compression energy. Because pipelines are discrete assets, the cost optimum may occur by accepting a small energy-yield loss if it avoids an additional pipeline.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
The PEM electrolyser stack is the primary energy conversion component of the hydrogen production system. It converts electrical power and water into hydrogen and oxygen and therefore largely determines the overall efficiency of the electrolyser.
Within this model, the stack is represented explicitly because its efficiency, degradation and sizing have a strong influence on the optimal design of the offshore energy system. Rather than optimising the stack in isolation, it is evaluated as one component of the complete offshore hydrogen production chain.
PEM stacks are present in both centralised and decentralised hydrogen production architectures.






NoteWhy PEM?



PEM electrolysis is selected because it is well suited to variable renewable electricity. The technology can rapidly follow fluctuations in wind power while maintaining high efficiency over a wide operating range.
Another important advantage is that hydrogen is produced at an elevated outlet pressure (approximately 30 bar in the source material), reducing the required downstream compression ratio compared with low-pressure electrolysis technologies.
See the Compressor page for more discussion.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Stack Model
The stack model consists of four interacting components:

stack efficiency
modular operation
degradation
cost

Together these determine the optimal installed stack capacity and operating strategy.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Polarisation Curve
Engineering principle
The electrical energy required to produce hydrogen depends on the cell voltage. As current density increases, the cell voltage rises because activation, ohmic and mass transport losses become larger. Consequently, stack efficiency decreases at higher current densities.
Model implementation
Stack efficiency is calculated from a manufacturer polarisation curve (Manufacturer G, n.d.) relating cell voltage to current density. The operating point is defined as a percentage of the maximum current density (equivalently the maximum stack power).






Figure 1: Manufacturer polarisation curve (left) and resulting stack efficiency (right) used in the model.



As shown in Figure 1, the optimisation therefore captures the trade-off between operating fewer stacks at high current density or more stacks at lower current density.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Modularity
Commercial PEM electrolysers are typically manufactured as modular units with capacities of approximately 1 MW. Larger electrolysers are constructed by combining many identical modules.
The modular approach offers several practical advantages:

repeatable manufacturing
manageable electrical voltages and currents
improved thermal management
easier transport and installation
simplified maintenance and replacement

The model therefore represents an electrolyser as a collection of identical stack modules.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Module Switching
Because the electrolyser is modular, not every stack module has to operate simultaneously.
For every operating point, the model selects the number of active modules that maximises the overall conversion efficiency. The available electrical power is then distributed across the active modules.
This operational flexibility also alleviates the minimum-load limitation of PEM stacks, which is typically around 10% of the rated module capacity.
For example, a 10 MW electrolyser consisting of ten 1 MW modules can operate at only one active module and 10% load. The minimum system load therefore becomes approximately 100 kW rather than 1 MW, allowing hydrogen production to continue during periods of low wind generation without operating individual stacks below their safe operating limit.
Module switching is assumed to occur without efficiency or lifetime penalties.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Stack Overplanting
The modular architecture naturally allows installation of more stack capacity than the maximum available electrical input. This is referred to here as stack overplanting.
Operating a larger installed stack capacity reduces the average current density of each active module. Lower current density increases conversion efficiency and slows stack degradation.
These benefits come at the expense of additional stack CAPEX. The model therefore treats the installed stack capacity as an optimisation variable and determines the economically optimal degree of overplanting by minimising the overall LCOE.
In this LCOE optimisation, the system scope greatly influences the outcome. As the scope expands, the optimum generally shifts towards larger stack capacities and higher efficiencies, as stack costs become a smaller fraction of the total system investment. See the box below for a worked example.






NoteExample: Why the optimisation scope matters



Consider first an electrolyser system consisting only of the power electronics, stacks and balance of plant.
If the stack represents roughly 30% of the total electrolyser cost, increasing the installed stack capacity by 50% increases the overall system CAPEX by approximately 15%. Such an investment is only justified when the resulting efficiency improvement produces comparable lifetime savings.
Now consider the complete offshore hydrogen production system, including wind turbines, electrical infrastructure, offshore installation and export systems.
Within this larger system the stack may represent only 5% of the total investment A 50% increase in installed stack capacity therefore increases total project cost by only around 2.5%, making relatively small efficiency improvements economically worthwhile.
This illustrates why component optimisation should always be performed within the context of the complete energy system rather than considering each component independently.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Degradation
Efficiency loss
PEM stacks gradually degrade during operation. As degradation progresses, the cell voltage increases, reducing the electrical efficiency of hydrogen production. The model assumes linear degradation with accumulated full-load operating hours at a rate of 0.18% per 1000 full-load hours.
Stack replacement
Eventually the efficiency loss becomes sufficiently large that replacing the stack is economically preferable to continued operation. Rather than prescribing a fixed replacement criterion, the replacement moment is determined through the LCOH optimisation. In practice, approximately 10% performance degradation is commonly considered end-of-life.
Effect of partial-load operation
Operating more installed stack capacity reduces the average current density of each module, slowing degradation and extending stack lifetime. This creates an additional economic incentive for stack overplanting, alongside the efficiency improvements described previously.






NoteExample: Stack overplanting and degradation



Assume a stack is replaced after reaching 10% degradation. With a degradation rate of 0.18% per 1000 full-load hours, replacement occurs after approximately 58,500 full-load hours. Assuming an offshore wind capacity factor of 40%, this corresponds to roughly 16.7 calendar years. A 25-year project therefore requires at least one stack replacement. If this replacement is already unavoidable, installing additional stack capacity from the outset becomes an attractive alternative. The total stack material requirement over the project lifetime remains similar, while the system additionally benefits from:

Lower maintenance costs by avoiding mid-life replacement.
Higher efficiency through operation at lower current density.
Reduced degradation throughout the project lifetime.

This conclusion depends strongly on the assumption that degradation scales linearly with accumulated full-load hours.

title: Stack (PEM)
text:
Cost Model
Cost basis
The stack cost is based on the NREL bottom-up manufactured cost analysis for PEM water electrolyser stacks (Badgett et al. 2024). The NREL study evaluates a 1 MW PEM electrolyser stack and reports stack manufactured costs in 2020 US dollars per kW of stack capacity. The reported stack-only manufactured costs are:

316 $/kW at 10 MW/year manufacturing volume
183 $/kW at 100 MW/year manufacturing volume
164 $/kW at 1,000 MW/year manufacturing volume

These values exclude manufacturer markup, installation costs, soft costs and inflation. They are therefore used here as stack manufacturing cost inputs rather than complete installed electrolyser system costs.
For the base case, the model uses the 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case, corresponding to a stack manufactured cost of 164 $/kW in the NREL reference case. This case is selected because the offshore hydrogen system considered here represents industrial-scale deployment rather than early low-volume manufacturing. The 10 MW/year and 100 MW/year cases may be used in sensitivity analysis to represent less mature supply chains or slower manufacturing scale-up.
Reference-rated stack capacity
A complication is that the rated power of a PEM stack is not a purely physical property. For a given number of cells and active cell area, stack power depends on the current density at which the stack is rated. A higher rated current density gives more electrical power from the same physical stack and therefore reduces the apparent cost expressed in $/kW or €/MW, even if the stack itself has not become cheaper.
This is important because current density is treated explicitly in this model. Operating at higher current density increases the power output of a given stack, but it also increases cell voltage, reduces efficiency and accelerates degradation. Conversely, installing more stack capacity allows operation at lower current density, improving efficiency and lifetime at the expense of higher CAPEX.
The model therefore uses a reference-rated stack capacity as the cost-normalisation convention. This is the electrical capacity the installed stack would have if operated at a fixed reference current density of 3 A/cm². The reference-rated capacity is used only for cost accounting; it does not imply that the stack must operate continuously at this current density.
NREL’s cost values are converted to this 3 A/cm² reference-rating convention where necessary. This avoids treating changes in rating current density as independent cost reductions. In the NREL cost-reduction waterfall, part of the reduction in $/kW arises from increased current density, because the same physical stack area is assigned a higher rated power. In this model, that mechanism is already captured explicitly through the polarisation curve: higher current density allows more power from the same installed stack, but with an efficiency and degradation penalty. Therefore, current-density-driven reductions in reported $/kW are not applied as a separate stack cost reduction.
Model implementation
The stack is modelled as a modular component whose cost scales linearly with installed reference-rated stack capacity. Linear scaling is used because larger PEM electrolyser systems are represented as multiple identical stack modules rather than as a single geometrically scaled stack. As a result, increasing installed stack capacity increases the number of modules, cells and active area approximately proportionally. No equipment-level scaling exponent is therefore applied to the stack itself.
Actual stack operation is determined separately by the optimisation. At each time step, the model chooses the number of active modules and their operating current density. The corresponding electrical input, hydrogen production, efficiency and degradation are calculated from the polarisation curve. Reference-rated stack capacity is therefore a bookkeeping convention for cost only, while the physical and operational behaviour of the stack remains governed by current density.
Cost development
The main cost reductions for PEM stacks are assumed to come from manufacturing learning, higher production volumes and material reductions rather than from size-based economies of scale at the individual-stack level. In the NREL analysis, increasing manufacturing volume from 10 MW/year to 1,000 MW/year reduces the reported stack manufactured cost from 316 $/kW to 164 $/kW.
However, cost reductions associated purely with higher rated current density are treated separately from manufacturing learning. A higher current density reduces the reported $/kW by increasing the rated power per unit active area, but it does not necessarily reduce the physical cost of the installed stack. However, in this research, the reference rated stack current density is 3 A/cm2, but NREL uses 2 A/cm2. So this cost reduction must be applied as well.
Taking figure 27 as the reference, we apply the increased current density to 3 A/cm2 and economies of scale to 1000 MW/year to find \(316-57-132-15=112\) $/kW. Consequently, a 50% manufacturers cost mark-up as well as conversion to 2024€ is applied to find: 100 €/kW (CHECK)
Scope distinction
Only the stack cost is included in this component model. Balance-of-plant equipment, power electronics, installation, offshore structures and other system-level costs are represented elsewhere in the model. This distinction is important because the NREL report also provides full electrolyser system costs, but those include balance-of-plant components that are outside the scope of this stack page.
Stack replacement costs are calculated using the same specific stack cost assumption as the initial stack.

Availability
The modular architecture provides inherent redundancy because individual stack modules can be isolated without shutting down the complete electrolyser. A stack availability of 99.5% is assumed throughout this study.

title: Power Electronics
text:
Reference Architecture
The reference configuration is a water-cooled, 24-pulse thyristor rectifier supplied through a phase-shifting rectifier transformer. Multi-pulse thyristor conversion remains a common industrial solution at multi-megawatt scale because it combines high efficiency, low semiconductor cost, high current capability, and established reliability. Contemporary commercial systems are offered in 6-, 12-, 18-, and 24-pulse arrangements, with harmonic distortion decreasing as pulse number increases (ABB 2025). Reviews of large-scale electrolyser converters likewise identify thyristor rectifiers as the established high-power option, while active-front-end and chopper-based systems trade higher cost and conversion complexity for improved power quality and controllability (Yodwong et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2022).
The 66 kV input is represented as an aggregated two-stage voltage reduction:
\[
66\ \mathrm{kV\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{medium\mbox{-}voltage\ AC}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{controlled\ stack\ DC}.
\]
The intermediate voltage and detailed transformer winding arrangement are not modelled. Large-plant studies use comparable high-voltage-to-medium-voltage distribution followed by repeated transformer–rectifier modules, including PEM layouts based on approximately 40 MW power blocks (Noordende and Ripson 2020).

title: Power Electronics
text:
Cost Basis
Published power-electronics costs are not fully like-for-like. The literature includes manufactured cost, purchased-equipment cost, and installed system cost, with different transformer and auxiliary-equipment boundaries. Where a source explicitly reports manufactured cost before markup, the same 50% manufacturer markup used for the stack and balance-of-plant costs is applied here before comparison (see Financial Assumptions), rather than treating any single source as a directly transferable quotation.
NREL adopts a cost of 199 USD/kW for the transformer and rectifier of a 1 MW PEM electrolyser, based on historical supplier quotations and explicitly excluding manufacturer markup, installation, soft costs, and inflation (Badgett et al. 2024). Applying the standard 50% markup gives an equipment purchase cost of:
\[
1.5 \times 199 \approx 300 \ \mathrm{USD_{2020}/kW}
\]
Fraunhofer ISE estimates PEM power-electronics costs of approximately 160 EUR/kW in its 2020 cases and approximately 101–102 EUR/kW in its 2030 cases, reported at the system/investment level rather than as a bare manufactured cost. Its 100 MW cases add a separate high-voltage transformer of approximately 25–26 EUR/kW, giving a combined large-system estimate of approximately 185–186 EUR/kW. The specific cost of the power electronics changes only marginally between the 5 MW and 100 MW cases (Holst et al. 2021). A recent industrial comparison reports substantially lower Chinese-market investment costs for 5 MW packages: approximately CNY 270/kW for a thyristor rectifier including its phase-shifting transformer, compared with CNY 320/kW for a diode-plus-chopper system and CNY 400/kW for an IGBT system (Gao et al. 2025). No CNY-to-EUR conversion is applied here: the comparison is used only to confirm that thyristor rectifiers are the lower-cost topology, not as a quantitative anchor, because the geography, project scope, installation boundary, and procurement conditions differ too much for a direct rate conversion to be meaningful.
No public vendor source was found that provides a binding price for a complete offshore 66 kV-to-DC package with a consistent scope. Vendor literature is therefore used to confirm topology, modularity, and efficiency, but not as the primary cost basis.
The central model value is 185 EUR/kW for the complete purchased 66 kV-to-stack-DC conversion package, taken directly from Fraunhofer’s combined large-system transformer-plus-power-electronics estimate. This sits well below the marked-up NREL benchmark of approximately 300 USD/kW for a small 1 MW reference unit — compared here at face value, pending a documented USD-to-EUR conversion factor (see Financial Assumptions) — and above the lowest reported regional equipment prices.

title: Power Electronics
text:
Cost Scaling
No six-tenths-rule scaling is applied. The subsystem is treated as repeated transformer–rectifier power blocks, giving a scaling exponent of 1.00.
This assumption is based on practical unit limits rather than an assumption that electrical equipment has no economies of scale. Industrial rectifiers operate at very high current and are built from parallel semiconductor devices and repeated bridges because a single device cannot supply the complete plant current (Gao et al. 2025). Commercial high-power converter units are typically limited to the multi-megawatt range, after which plant capacity is increased mainly by adding modules (Chen et al. 2022). Large electrolyser designs similarly number up repeated stack and transformer–rectifier blocks rather than enlarging one converter indefinitely (Noordende and Ripson 2020).
Fraunhofer’s bottom-up results support this approximation: specific power-electronics cost is nearly constant between 5 MW and 100 MW, unlike centralised process equipment that benefits more strongly from shared capacity (Holst et al. 2021). Some plant-level economies can still arise from shared engineering, controls, switchgear, buildings, and procurement. The exponent of 1.00 should therefore be interpreted as a conservative purchased-equipment assumption, not proof that total installed electrical-system cost is perfectly linear.

The value represents a modern, high-efficiency thyristor package rather than a generic historical fleet average. Scaling Method
The BOP is not assumed to scale linearly with installed capacity. Water treatment, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, piping and instrumentation can be shared across multiple stacks. A centralised or semi-centralised BOP system is therefore expected to be cheaper than many small independent BOP systems with the same total capacity.
Because the exact scaling exponent is not known, the model uses the six-tenths rule as a first-order process-equipment scaling approximation. The six-tenths rule is a standard preliminary process-equipment cost-scaling method in which cost scales with capacity using an exponent close to 0.6 (Engineering LibreTexts, n.d.; Peters et al., n.d.).

The offshore water treatment cost is scaled separately:
[ C_{,i} = C_ ( )^{0.6}]
The total BOP cost is calculated by summing the non-water BOP and offshore water treatment costs over all independent BOP units:
[ C_ = _i ]
This formulation allows the model to distinguish between decentralised and centralised electrolyser architectures.
Under this scaling assumption, a more centralised BOP architecture is cheaper than a highly decentralised architecture with the same total electrolyser capacity. In practice, the optimum is likely to involve several shared BOP trains rather than one fully centralised unit, because redundancy, maintainability and safety constraints limit the practical size of individual BOP systems.
The scaling rule should therefore be interpreted as an early-stage approximation rather than a detailed equipment design. Future work may replace this rule with a process-level BOP model for seawater intake, desalination, deionisation, cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying and hydrogen-side piping.

title: Hydrogen Infrastructure
text:
Hydrogen infrastructure covers everything that moves hydrogen from the electrolyser outlet to the onshore interface: compression, and the pipeline network that carries the gas offshore and to shore.
The section is split into:

Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure — ladder topology for the decentralised architecture and the calculation of total infield pipeline length.
Hydrogen Compressor — raises hydrogen from electrolyser outlet pressure to the pipeline injection pressure, with the associated electricity consumption, CAPEX, and OPEX.
Hydrogen Pipelines — composite flexible pipeline technology, diameter and pressure sizing, transport capacity, and material cost, for both the infield network and the export route.
Pipeline Pressure and Capacity — how pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and installation cost trade off against each other in sizing the pipeline system.

Compressor and pipeline assumptions are coupled rather than independent: higher inlet pressure increases compressor energy consumption and cost but also increases pipeline capacity, which can reduce the number of parallel pipelines required. Pipeline count in turn interacts with installation cost, because a single lay vessel can install multiple pipelines together. Pressure, diameter, and pipeline count are therefore optimised jointly rather than one at a time.
The current hydrogen infrastructure model assumes no additional hydrogen losses in pipelines after compression.

title: Hydrogen Pipelines
text:
Composite Flexible Pipelines
Composite flexible pipelines are used as the reference hydrogen pipeline technology in this model. A flexible composite pipe typically combines a hydrogen-compatible liner, load-bearing composite reinforcement, and a protective outer layer. Compared with a rigid steel pipeline, the relevant system-level advantage is not only material substitution. The important offshore feature is that the pipe can be manufactured and transported in long continuous lengths, spooled on a reel, and laid with fewer welded field joints.
This matters for offshore hydrogen infrastructure because the model is concerned with many repeated infield connections and, in the decentralised architecture, a pipeline grid that replaces the AC infield cable network. Flexible composite lines are lighter than steel lines at the diameters considered here, are less exposed to corrosion-related design issues, and can simplify installation logistics. These advantages are especially relevant for infield pipelines and for export pipelines up to the diameter range that remains compatible with reel-lay handling.
The flexibility benefit is not unlimited. Larger diameters and higher pressure classes require more reinforcement and increase minimum bend radius. The source material therefore caps the composite export-pipeline diameter at 8 inch: above this range, the pipeline is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that motivates the technology choice (Project Team 2026).

The current cost model covers material cost only. Installation, burial, connection, vessel time, lay-pass grouping and termination work are excluded here and treated in the shared installation section. More than one TCP pipeline per lay pass is not assumed without project-specific evidence.

Confidentiality Handling
The raw supplier quotes and fitted material-cost surface are confidential. They are used only to parameterise the model and are not reproduced in this encyclopedia page. Figures derived from them show pressure and diameter on their true scale, since those are model inputs, not supplier data. The cost axis is left without tick labels so that only the shape of the cost curves, not the underlying price level, is disclosed.


Material Cost vs. Pressure
Figure 2 shows pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure, for the same diameters used in Figure 1. Cost increases sharply from one diameter class to the next, which is expected for a larger pipe, but at fixed diameter the increase with pressure is comparatively small. Material cost, in other words, is mainly a diameter decision. It is capacity, not material cost, that responds strongly to pressure, which is why pressure and diameter play such different roles in the trade-off described in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: raising pressure is cheap on the pipe itself, and its real cost shows up at the compressor instead (Hydrogen Compressor).






Figure 2: Hydrogen export-pipeline material cost as a function of inlet pressure and diameter.





Cost per Unit of Transport Capacity
Figure 3 divides the cost curves in Figure 2 by the capacity curves in Figure 1, giving material cost per unit of transport capacity at each diameter and pressure.
Because capacity scales much more strongly with diameter than material cost does, cost per unit capacity falls as diameter increases. This is the basis for the earlier claim that the economic optimum tends toward the largest feasible composite diameter. The same ratio also falls with pressure, at diminishing rate, for the same reason: on the pipe alone, more pressure buys more capacity for very little extra material cost. This curve reflects material cost only. It does not include the compressor cost and energy penalty that pressure also brings, which is why a pure cost-per-capacity view of the pipeline cannot be used to pick a pressure on its own — see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how the compressor side of that trade-off is brought back in.

title: Infield AC Cables
section: Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
text:
Why 66 kV Is the Reference Voltage
Moving from 33 kV to 66 kV approximately doubles the transferable power at the same current. That allows more turbine capacity per string, fewer strings and fewer offshore-platform entries. Carbon Trust estimated that the transition could reduce offshore-wind LCOE by about 1.5%, and DNV GL’s TenneT study found a material reduction in cable length for the Dutch Borssele concept (Carbon Trust 2014; DNV GL 2015).
The technology is now demonstrated at commercial scale. Borssele 1 and 2 used three-phase 66 kV copper array cables in two cross-sections over roughly 170–190 km (Nexans 2018). Fixed 66 kV-class submarine cables fall within the scope of IEC 63026, while project design must also address offshore-specific interfaces, installation and mechanical loading (International Electrotechnical Commission 2019; DNV, n.d.).
66 kV should nevertheless be treated as the current reference, not a permanent optimum. Carbon Trust’s later high-voltage-array work considers 132 kV as turbine and plant ratings grow; it reported modelled savings of GBP 32–50 million for a 1,200 MW future plant relative to an equivalent 66 kV system (Carbon Trust 2022).

text:
String Capacity Model
For target farm capacity \(P_\mathrm{target}\) and turbine rating \(P_\mathrm{turb}\), the installed turbine count and capacity are:
\[
N_\mathrm{turb}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{P_\mathrm{target}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rceil,
\qquad
P_\mathrm{farm}
=
N_\mathrm{turb}P_\mathrm{turb}.
\]
For a selected usable string rating, the number of full turbines that fit on one radial string is:
\[
n_\mathrm{turb/string}
=
\left\lfloor
\frac{P_\mathrm{string}}{P_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rfloor,
\]
and the minimum number of strings is:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{N_\mathrm{turb}}{n_\mathrm{turb/string}}
\right\rceil.
\]
The floor operator in the first equation prevents a fraction of a turbine being assigned to a string. The ceiling operator in the second ensures that a partly filled final string still receives a complete cable, switchgear bay and platform termination. These discrete jumps are why a small change in turbine or string rating can create a noticeable CAPEX step.
This is the same basic capacity logic used by NREL’s ORBIT model (Nunemaker et al. 2020). Final cable selection must also check voltage drop, short-circuit duty, charging current, burial depth, seabed thermal resistivity, conductor temperature, armour losses and post-installation protection.






NoteWorked example: 15 MW turbines



Four 15 MW turbines place 60 MW on a string. Five place 75 MW on it and exceed the 64–66 MW screening range. A nominal 2 GW target therefore requires 134 turbines, giving 2.01 GW installed and:
\[
n_\mathrm{string}=\left\lceil\frac{134}{4}\right\rceil=34.
\]


Figure 1 shows the resulting discrete string count. A small increase in plant capacity can require a complete additional feeder, switchgear bay, J-tube, pull-in and cable route.






Figure 1: Required 66 kV radial strings for 15 MW turbines and a 64–66 MW usable string rating.









WarningThe worked array does not fit the reference platform unchanged



TenneT’s 2 GW reference arrangement shows 24 dedicated wind-farm bays plus four universal bays (TenneT 2024). The 34-string worked case therefore needs at least six more terminations than the maximum 28 shown, even if every universal bay is assigned to a feeder. A consistent design must do one or more of the following:

adopt a cable and platform interface rated for at least 75 MW per string, so five 15 MW turbines fit and only 27 strings are required;
add offshore feeder aggregation or another switchgear interface;
move to a higher collection voltage; or
use a project-specific platform layout with more bays.

This interface constraint must be solved before the 34-string cable count and standard 2 GW platform are combined in one cost case.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Cable-Length Model
Cable length is calculated from the modelled turbine layout and radial-string topology. Capacity determines the number of turbines and strings; rotor diameter and spacing determine their separation; farm area, aspect ratio and substation position constrain the coordinates. This keeps cable length responsive when any of those design inputs change.
For rotor diameter \(D\) in metres and along-string and cross-string spacings \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) in rotor diameters, the physical spacings are:
\[
d_x=\frac{s_xD}{1000},
\qquad
d_y=\frac{s_yD}{1000},
\]
where \(d_x\) and \(d_y\) are in kilometres. The wind-layout model places \(N_\mathrm{turb}\) turbines inside the farm boundary using these spacings and returns turbine coordinates \((x_j,y_j)\). The gross farm area \(A_\mathrm{farm}\), spacing and turbine count are not independent: the selected coordinates must satisfy both the minimum-spacing rules and the site boundary. The model must flag an infeasible combination rather than silently rescale the spacing.
For an ideal rectangular grid with \(n_x\) turbine positions along the wind direction and \(n_y\) across it, where \(n_xn_y\geq N_\mathrm{turb}\), the occupied grid spans are:
\[
W_\mathrm{grid}=(n_x-1)d_x,
\qquad
H_\mathrm{grid}=(n_y-1)d_y.
\]
These spans, together with boundary margins and exclusions, must fit inside \(A_\mathrm{farm}\). Farm area is therefore a geometric constraint, not an additional cable-length multiplier. A larger boundary changes cable length only when the layout actually spreads the turbine coordinates farther apart.
The string-capacity calculation above partitions the turbines into radial strings with no more than \(n_\mathrm{turb/string}\) turbines. Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be the resulting set of cable connections: one connection from the offshore substation to the first turbine on each string, followed by turbine-to-turbine connections. The horizontal distance of connection \((u,v)\) is:
\[
d_{uv}
=
\sqrt{(x_u-x_v)^2+(y_u-y_v)^2}.
\]
Total pre-route horizontal cable length is therefore:
\[
L_\mathrm{horizontal}
=
\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}d_{uv},
\]
and the screening supply length is:
\[
L_\mathrm{array}
=
(1+r)L_\mathrm{horizontal}
+
L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in},
\]
where \(r\) is the route allowance and \(L_\mathrm{pull\text{-}in}\) is the separately calculated total cable length between seabed touchdown points and turbine or platform terminations. No default pull-in length is inserted until the water-depth and interface assumptions are defined.
This is the same calculation structure used by ORBIT’s grid-array model: turbine and row spacing define coordinates, cable capacity limits turbines per string, and the model sums the Euclidean distance between successive connection points (Nunemaker et al. 2020).

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
OPEX Allowance
Public evidence describes large but infrequent cable failures more clearly than it reports expected annual cable-only expenditure. ORE Catapult’s SPARTA portfolio found cable outages in 7.46% of wind-farm months and in 61% of reporting wind farms, with outage days split approximately equally between array and export cables (ORE Catapult 2022). Its ELECTRODE programme reports an average repair duration of about two months and consequences often above GBP 10 million, but that amount combines repair expenditure and lost generation (ORE Catapult 2023).
These data do not provide an array-only annual failure frequency or a clean split between physical repair cost and lost revenue. An event-based OPEX model is therefore not used. The current relationship is retained as a top-down risk allowance:
\[
C_\mathrm{OPEX}
=
f_\mathrm{OPEX}C_\mathrm{supply},
\]
with \(f_\mathrm{OPEX}=2\%\)/year and a 1–3% sensitivity. At the base cable price, each 100 km of supplied cable has EUR 40 million supply CAPEX and therefore a EUR 0.8 million annual allowance. The allowance represents inspection and physical repair provision only. Lost generation remains in the availability calculation and must not also be included in OPEX.

title: Infield AC Cables
text:
Reliability and Availability
The current model applies 99.0% array-network availability as a flat annual yield multiplier. A radial string fault normally disconnects the turbines downstream of the fault rather than the complete wind farm, so the flat multiplier does not represent topology explicitly.
No more detailed failure model is introduced until consistent array-specific failure frequency, repair duration and affected-capacity data are available. When those inputs exist, the radial connections \(\mathcal{E}\) defined by the cable-length model can also define the turbines isolated by each fault. Until then, 99.0% remains a transparent aggregate assumption rather than a calculated reliability result.

title: About
text:
This site documents the assumptions behind a component-level techno-economic model for offshore wind infrastructure.
The model compares electricity-based export, centralised offshore hydrogen production, and decentralised turbine-integrated hydrogen production. The documentation here is limited to methodology and assumptions: system boundaries, component cost models, energy balances, availability factors, installation assumptions, and shared financial conventions.
The source material is a set of working Word documents in background/. Some assumptions rely on internal supplier or manufacturer data; those are documented at the level needed for model reproducibility without exposing confidential raw datasets.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Physical Layout
At landfall, the submarine cable is brought ashore through an open trench or, more commonly at sensitive coastlines, ducts installed by horizontal directional drilling. Submarine and land cable designs are connected in accessible transition-joint bays. The separate pole, metallic-return and communication cables then continue underground to the converter site.
The onshore converter changes DC power back to three-phase AC. Converter transformers provide voltage transformation and electrical separation, while reactors, filters and controls manage current, harmonics, voltage and reactive power. High-voltage switchgear connects the station to the transmission grid and isolates equipment for faults and maintenance.
TenneT describes the Dutch 2 GW interface as 525 kV DC conversion to 380 kV AC. Its standard onshore arrangement has six single-phase converter transformers plus one spare (TenneT 2024). For the Doordewind connection, TenneT reports an onshore converter-station footprint of roughly 5.5 ha before the underground connection to the 380 kV substation (TenneT, n.d.). The land requirement reflects electrical clearances, converter halls, cooling, transformers, roads, drainage, security and construction space; it is not just the building footprint.

title: Onshore Grid Connection
text:
Electrical Rating
AC equipment must carry more than active MW alone:

active power \(P\), measured in MW, transfers net energy and is what the wind farm is primarily selling;
reactive power \(Q\), measured in MVAr, oscillates between electric and magnetic fields and is used to control AC voltage; and
apparent power \(S\), measured in MVA, combines both and determines much of the current and thermal loading of transformers, converters and switchgear.

Power factor is \(P/S\). A value below one means some equipment current is being used for reactive rather than active power.
At unity power factor, the AC line current associated with 2 GW at 380 kV is:
\[
I_\mathrm{AC}
=
\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_\mathrm{LL}\cos\phi}
=
\frac{2{,}000\times10^6}
{\sqrt{3}(380\times10^3)}
=3.04\ \mathrm{kA}.
\]
The station is not designed as one 3 kA conductor. Power is divided among converter transformer windings, bus sections and grid circuits so equipment ratings, fault levels and maintenance criteria can be satisfied.
Reactive-power operation increases apparent power:
\[
S=\frac{P}{\cos\phi},
\qquad
Q=\sqrt{S^2-P^2}.
\]
If 2 GW were delivered at a power factor of 0.95, the terminal duty would be about 2.105 GVA and 657 MVAr. This is an illustration, not a selected grid-code operating point. Actual reactive capability is specified as a voltage-dependent envelope and can require converter-current headroom, reactors or additional compensation.
The grid-connection study must check at least:

rated and temporary voltage ranges;
active-power ramping and frequency response;
reactive-power and voltage-control capability;
fault ride-through and post-fault active-power recovery;
harmonic emission and resonance;
short-circuit level and protection coordination;
maximum permissible loss of infeed.

Several of these terms describe different questions. Fault level is the current the surrounding grid can supply into a short circuit; it affects switchgear duty and converter-control behaviour, not how often faults occur. Fault ride-through asks whether the link remains connected during a temporary voltage depression. Harmonics are unwanted waveform components that can cause heating, resonance or interference. A strong grid node is one whose voltage and stability remain acceptable when 2 GW changes or trips–not merely one with high annual energy demand.
Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/1447 sets the European HVDC framework for these active-power, reactive-power, voltage, fault-ride-through, control, protection and monitoring capabilities (European Commission 2016). Project-specific requirements are then agreed with the relevant transmission-system operator.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
The hydrogen compressor raises the pressure of produced hydrogen from the PEM electrolyser outlet pressure to the pressure required by the hydrogen pipeline system.
The compressor is modelled explicitly because the pipeline injection pressure is a decision variable in this research. The model must therefore capture how compressor energy consumption and compressor cost change when the selected outlet pressure changes. This is necessary for the pressure-diameter optimisation of the hydrogen pipeline system.
Compression is included only in the hydrogen architectures. In the centralised architecture, compression takes place on the offshore electrolysis platform before injection into the export pipeline. In the decentralised architecture, compression takes place at turbine level before injection into the infield hydrogen pipeline.
The compressor model includes compressor electricity consumption, motor losses, CAPEX, OPEX and availability. It excludes electrolyser stack costs, electrolyser BOP, hydrogen drying, pipeline CAPEX, pipeline pressure drop and onshore recompression.






NoteWhy Outlet Pressure Is Modelled Explicitly



The compressor outlet pressure is the pipeline injection pressure, one of the optimisation variables in this research. Raising it trades cheaper, higher-capacity pipeline transport against a larger compressor energy and CAPEX penalty; see Pipeline Pressure and Capacity for how that trade-off plays out against pipeline diameter, pipeline count, and installation cost.
A fixed compressor energy value would hide that trade-off from the optimisation. This page therefore develops explicit compressor energy and cost models as a function of inlet pressure, outlet pressure, and hydrogen mass flow, so that the optimisation has something to weigh the pipeline side against. See Compression Energy and Cost Model below.

Compressing from 1 bar to 150 bar has a pressure ratio of 150. This is why the relatively high outlet pressure of PEM electrolysers is important for offshore hydrogen systems.

title: Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Compression Energy
The number of compression stages is determined from the maximum allowable pressure ratio per stage:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(p_\mathrm{out}/p_\mathrm{in})}
{\ln(r_\mathrm{max})}
\right\rceil
\]
where \(r_\mathrm{max}=3.3\).
The actual pressure ratio per stage is:
\[
r_s =
\left(
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\right)^{1/N}
\]
For the reference case of compression from 30 bar to 150 bar:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
=
\frac{150}{30}
=
5
\]
This gives:
\[
N =
\left\lceil
\frac{\ln(5)}{\ln(3.3)}
\right\rceil
=
2
\]
and:
\[
r_s = 5^{1/2} = 2.24
\]
The compressor shaft work per kg of hydrogen is calculated as:
\[
w_\mathrm{shaft} =
\frac{
N \gamma Z_\mathrm{avg} R T
}{
(\gamma - 1) M_\mathrm{H_2} \eta_\mathrm{comp}
}
\left[
r_s^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} - 1
\right]
\]
where \(Z_\mathrm{avg}\) is the average hydrogen compressibility factor between inlet and outlet pressure, evaluated from real-gas hydrogen properties via CoolProp at the arithmetic mean of \(p_\mathrm{in}\) and \(p_\mathrm{out}\), the same way the pipeline capacity model evaluates gas properties at an average pipeline pressure. Hydrogen deviates only mildly from ideal-gas behaviour over this pressure range (\(Z_\mathrm{avg}\) stays within a few percent of 1), but the deviation is calculated rather than assumed.
The electrical energy consumption of the compressor is:
\[
e_\mathrm{comp} =
\frac{
w_\mathrm{shaft}
}{
\eta_\mathrm{motor} \cdot 3.6 \cdot 10^6
}
\]
where \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is expressed in kWh/kg H₂.
The compressor power demand is then calculated from the hydrogen mass flow rate:
\[
P_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
where \(P_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kW when \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) is in kWh/kg H₂ and \(\dot{m}_\mathrm{H_2}\) is in kg/h.
For annual or time-step calculations, total compressor electricity use is:
\[
E_\mathrm{comp}
=
e_\mathrm{comp}
\cdot
m_\mathrm{H_2}
\]
This energy use is treated as a parasitic load in the hydrogen system.

Sensitivity to Outlet Pressure
Compressor energy consumption increases with outlet pressure because the relevant quantity is the pressure ratio:
\[
\frac{p_\mathrm{out}}{p_\mathrm{in}}
\]
The same outlet pressure can therefore have very different compression penalties depending on electrolyser outlet pressure. Compression to 150 bar is a relatively modest duty when hydrogen leaves the PEM electrolyser at 30 bar, but a much larger duty if hydrogen is produced near atmospheric pressure.
Figure 1 shows \(e_\mathrm{comp}\) across the 80-150 bar outlet-pressure range used elsewhere in the model, for electrolyser outlet pressures of 1, 10, 20 and 30 bar.






Figure 1: Compressor electricity consumption as a function of outlet pressure for different inlet pressures.



The curves confirm why PEM outlet pressure matters: at a given pipeline injection pressure, compressing from 1 bar takes roughly three to four and a half times the electricity of compressing from 30 bar, because it is the pressure ratio that drives compression work, not the absolute pressure difference. Each curve also shows small kinks rather than a smooth rise. These come from the discrete number of compression stages, \(N\): as outlet pressure increases, \(N\) occasionally steps up to keep the per-stage pressure ratio within its 3.3 limit, and each step changes the slope of the curve.

Hydrogen Compressor
text:
Pressure Optimisation
Pipeline injection pressure is optimised together with pipeline diameter and the number of parallel pipelines, for the reasons set out in Pipeline Pressure and Capacity: pressure, diameter, material cost, and installation cost all move together, so none of them can be picked in isolation.
The optimisation problem is therefore not:
\[
\min e_\mathrm{comp}
\]
and it is also not:
\[
\min C_\mathrm{pipeline}
\]
Instead, the model minimises the combined system cost:
\[
\min_{p_\mathrm{out}, D, n_\mathrm{pipe}}
LCOE
\]
where \(p_\mathrm{out}\) is compressor outlet pressure and pipeline injection pressure, \(D\) is pipeline diameter and \(n_\mathrm{pipe}\) is the number of parallel pipelines.
The optimum can therefore occur at an intermediate pressure. A higher pressure may be justified if it avoids an extra pipeline. A lower pressure may be preferable if the pipeline is already oversized and additional compression provides little transport benefit.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Proposed Ladder Layout
The proposed network is a ladder. Two longitudinal header pipelines run along opposite sides of the turbine field. Cross-farm pipelines form the rungs. Turbines connect directly to the rung that passes through their row.






Figure 1: Proposed hydrogen infield ladder. The number of rungs and turbines shown is schematic.



The layout is used for four reasons:

A 6 inch composite pipeline at 150 bar is assumed to carry about 500 MW of hydrogen on an HHV-equivalent basis. One rung can therefore collect a complete turbine row without the 60–70 MW string limit of a 66 kV AC cable (Project Team 2026).
Each turbine can send hydrogen to either header. Isolation of one local rung or header segment does not automatically isolate every turbine behind that segment.
The regular grid follows the turbine rows and avoids a separate radial route from every turbine to a central platform.
Flexible composite pipe can be supplied in long reeled lengths. This suits repeated infield runs and reduces the number of offshore field joints relative to rigid steel pipe (Project Team 2026).

The topology provides two infield paths, not two independent export systems. Both paths ultimately reach the same export-pipeline interface. Valves, isolation philosophy and the capacity of the remaining path determine whether the redundancy can be used after a fault.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Pipeline-Length Model
The screening model assumes:

a square wind-farm area;
evenly spaced turbines arranged in approximately square rows;
two headers, each equal to one farm side;
each rung spans one farm side; and
the number of rungs is approximated by the square root of turbine count.

For farm area \(A_\mathrm{farm}\) in km\(^2\), the side length is:
\[
s=\sqrt{A_\mathrm{farm}}.
\]
For \(N_\mathrm{turb}\) turbines, the continuous estimate of rung count is:
\[
n_\mathrm{rung}=\sqrt{N_\mathrm{turb}}.
\]
Rung length and header length are:
\[
L_\mathrm{rungs}
=
n_\mathrm{rung}s,
\qquad
L_\mathrm{headers}
=
2s.
\]
The total horizontal infield pipeline length is therefore:
\[
\boxed{
L_\mathrm{infield}
=
\sqrt{A_\mathrm{farm}}
\left(
\sqrt{N_\mathrm{turb}}+2
\right)
}
\]
with \(L_\mathrm{infield}\) in km when \(A_\mathrm{farm}\) is in km\(^2\) (Project Team 2026).
This continuous form is suitable for optimisation. A physical layout requires an integer number of rows. For a conservative square-grid representation, use:
\[
n_\mathrm{rung,int}
=
\left\lceil
\sqrt{N_\mathrm{turb}}
\right\rceil,
\qquad
L_\mathrm{infield,int}
=
\sqrt{A_\mathrm{farm}}
\left(
n_\mathrm{rung,int}+2
\right).
\]

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Reference Calculation
The reference farm has an area of 200 km\(^2\) and a nominal capacity of 2 GW. With 15 MW turbines, the required turbine count is:
\[
N_\mathrm{turb}
=
\left\lceil
\frac{2{,}000}{15}
\right\rceil
=
134.
\]
The farm side length and continuous rung estimate are:
\[
s=\sqrt{200}=14.142\ \mathrm{km},
\qquad
n_\mathrm{rung}=\sqrt{134}=11.576.
\]
The modelled pipeline length is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
L_\mathrm{infield}
&=
14.142(11.576+2) \\
&=
\boxed{192.0\ \mathrm{km}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If the layout is represented with 12 complete rungs:
\[
L_\mathrm{infield,int}
=
14.142(12+2)
=
\boxed{198.0\ \mathrm{km}}.
\]
The optimisation model should use 192.0 km if it retains the continuous approximation. A routed design with 12 physical rows should start from 198.0 km before project-specific adjustments.

title: Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
Hydrogen Infield Infrastructure
text:
Capacity and Redundancy Checks
The length equation defines geometry only. It does not prove that every segment can carry the required flow.
The 500 MW-equivalent assumption supports the claim that one 6 inch rung can serve a turbine row. Header flow is higher because successive rungs add hydrogen. Header diameter, pressure drop and fault-state capacity must therefore be checked segment by segment. The current model does not yet perform this check and should not assume that every header segment can remain 6 inch.
The same limitation applies to redundancy. An alternative route is useful only if isolation valves can separate the failed section and the remaining pipeline path has enough capacity. The present assumption of 100% infield-pipeline availability is a modelling convention, not a reliability result.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. They are three different ways of buying the same thing — hydrogen transport capacity — and each buys it through a different cost centre: pipe material, compressor equipment and energy, or installation. This page sets out how those three costs interact and why the resulting optimum is not smooth.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text: Pipeline diameter, inlet pressure, and the number of parallel pipelines are not independent choices. They are three different ways of buying the same thing — hydrogen transport capacity — and each buys it through a different cost centre: pipe material, compressor equipment and energy, or installation. This page sets out how those three costs interact and why the resulting optimum is not smooth.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Two Ways to Add Capacity
For a fixed pipeline, transport capacity increases with both diameter and pressure drop, but not at the same rate. Diameter enters the capacity relation through the cross-sectional area and the flow velocity together, so capacity scales approximately as \(D^{2.5}\). Pressure enters only through the pressure drop under a square root, so its effect is far weaker and subject to diminishing returns (full derivation in Hydrogen Pipelines).
This asymmetry means diameter and pressure are not equally good levers for the same job, and it is why the two behave so differently in the cost model, not just in the capacity model:

Increasing diameter is the more capacity-effective lever, but it is a step change in material commitment. A larger composite pipeline costs more per metre, and above roughly 8 inch the pipe is assumed to lose the reel-lay flexibility that keeps composite installation cheap in the first place (Hydrogen Pipelines). Past that point, diameter is no longer a lever that can be pulled without also changing the installation method and the cost basis that goes with it.
Increasing pressure adds capacity without any new material or route, but it is equipment- and energy-expensive at the compressor: every bar of additional pressure raises compressor CAPEX and adds a recurring electricity cost for the life of the asset (Hydrogen Compressor).

The same capacity requirement can therefore be met by a fatter pipe running at modest pressure, or a narrower pipe pushed harder by a larger compressor. Which is cheaper is not a property of the pipeline alone; it depends on how the pipe’s material-cost curve compares with the compressor’s cost-and-energy curve over the feasible pressure range.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
text:
Where Installation Cost Enters
Material and compression are not the whole story, because pipeline capacity is delivered in discrete units. A given diameter-pressure combination yields a fixed maximum flow; if peak hydrogen production exceeds it, the model does not fractionally upsize the pipe — it adds another parallel pipeline. That step adds physical pipe length, interfaces, vessel loads and installation passes.
Installation cost still does not scale as a simple EUR/m coefficient. Parallel lines may share engineering, mobilisation and one broader contractor programme, but each additional line increases the physical installation inventory. The current evidence supports one TCP pipeline per actual lay pass; simultaneous installation of several pipelines must not be assumed without supplier and contractor proof (Cable and Pipeline Installation).
The installation subclass is also tied to the diameter decision. It applies only while the selected pipe remains hydrogen-qualified and compatible with its reel, bend, tension, stability and pull-through limits. Crossing one of those limits can change the vessel, connection concept or pipe technology. Pushing diameter up to avoid another parallel line can therefore trade the discrete cost of an additional pass for a different installation subclass.

title: Pipeline Pressure and Capacity
section: The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
text:
The Resulting Trade-off Is Not Smooth
Because pipeline count is a ceiling function of required capacity, a small change in peak flow, diameter, or pressure can push a design across the threshold where an extra parallel pipeline becomes necessary — or unnecessary. Near that threshold, the marginal cost of “one more unit of capacity” jumps discontinuously: it can mean a small increase in compressor duty on the existing pipelines, or an entire additional pipeline’s material, interfaces, loads and installation passes.
This is why pressure, diameter, and pipeline count cannot be optimised one at a time. Raising pressure to avoid an extra pipeline only pays off if the resulting compressor cost and energy penalty are smaller than that pipeline’s material and subclass-specific installation cost. Conversely, adding a pipeline only pays off if its complete incremental cost is lower than the compressor cost of reaching the same capacity through pressure alone. The three variables have to be searched jointly over a cost landscape with discrete steps rather than solved as a single continuous minimum.

title: DC Integration
text:
The decentralised-hydrogen architecture directly couples a wind-turbine generator to a PEM electrolyser through a shared DC system. The model uses this configuration to remove conversion equipment that is only required for AC export or for supplying a conventional AC-fed electrolyser. The feasibility basis is the Hygro technical assessment of direct DC PEM-wind coupling (Verbist and Damen 2026).
The modelled electrical chain is:
wind-turbine generator -> active rectifier/up-chopper -> DC link -> PEM stack or stack array
The architecture has no AC export connection, turbine grid-side inverter, electrolyser rectifier, or separate electrolyser-side DC/DC converter. The generator-side active rectifier/up-chopper remains part of the turbine and controls generator current, electromagnetic torque, and the power extracted from the rotor.






NoteModel assumption



A dedicated electrolyser-side DC/DC converter is not treated as a fundamental requirement. Its functions are instead allocated to generator power control, generator-stack electrical matching, supervisory operating limits, and coordinated protection. This is an integrated turbine-electrolyser design assumption, not an off-the-shelf equipment configuration.

Its functions are instead allocated to generator power control, generator-stack electrical matching, supervisory operating limits, and coordinated protection. This is an integrated turbine-electrolyser design assumption, not an off-the-shelf equipment configuration.

title: DC Integration
text:
Operating Principle
The generator-side converter controls the electrical power supplied to the PEM system. The PEM polarisation characteristic then establishes the corresponding DC voltage and current. For a single stack, or the equivalent polarisation curve of the active stack array, the operating point satisfies:
\[
P_{\mathrm{gen}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}.
\]
where:

\(P_{\mathrm{gen}}\) is the generator electrical power supplied to the DC system, in W;
\(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) is the total current through the active stack configuration, in A; and
\(V_{\mathrm{stack}}(I_{\mathrm{stack}})\) is the voltage given by its polarisation curve at the applicable temperature, pressure, hydration state, tolerance, and age, in V.

As generator power rises or falls, the operating point moves along the applicable polarisation curve. The DC-link voltage is therefore an operating result rather than the primary controlled variable. Voltage is still measured for operating-envelope supervision, converter limits, and protection, but normal hydrogen production does not require a fixed DC-voltage reference.
This distinction replaces the previous page assumption that an active-front-end voltage loop must hold the DC link at a prescribed value. Even where an active rectifier is used, its normal control objective in this architecture is generator current, torque, and power.

title: DC Integration
text:
Model Calculation
At each operating point, the turbine power command is bounded by the available wind power, generator capability, and the power that the PEM system can safely accept:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
\min\!\left(
P_{\mathrm{wind,available}},
P_{\mathrm{gen,max}},
P_{\mathrm{PEM,permitted}}
\right).
\]
All four terms are powers in W. The permitted PEM power is a supervisory limit derived from current density, stack temperature and pressure, gas purity, water supply, cooling capacity, and the active stack configuration.
The electrical operating point is then found by solving:
\[
P_{\mathrm{cmd}}
=
V_{\mathrm{stack}}\!\left(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\right)
I_{\mathrm{stack}}
\]
within the permitted current and voltage range. The resulting \(I_{\mathrm{stack}}\) and \(V_{\mathrm{stack}}\) are passed to the PEM stack model to calculate hydrogen production, efficiency, and degradation.
If a modular stack array is used, branch switching changes the equivalent polarisation curve and provides coarse capacity selection. Generator torque remains the continuous power actuator.
